history.q: Who founded the Achaemenid Persian Empire in the 6th century BCE?
history.fact: The clay Cyrus Cylinder, now in the British Museum, records his capture of Babylon in 539 BCE and his restoration of its temples.

history.q: Which conqueror's army burned the palaces of Persepolis in 330 BCE?
history.fact: Ancient writers disagree on whether the fire was revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens or a drunken accident during a feast.

history.q: At which battle in 490 BCE did the Athenians defeat the invasion force sent by Darius I?
history.fact: Legend says a messenger ran about 40 km to Athens with news of the victory, inspiring the modern marathon race.

history.q: Which Persian king led the invasion of Greece that fought the Spartans at Thermopylae in 480 BCE?
history.fact: Xerxes' army crossed the Hellespont on bridges of boats, but his fleet was defeated at Salamis later that year.

history.q: In 1935 the government asked foreign nations to stop saying 'Persia' and use which name?
history.fact: Iranians had long called their land Iran; 'Persia' came from the Greek name for the southern province of Pars, today's Fars.

history.q: Who was Iran's last shah, who left the country in January 1979?
history.fact: Mohammad Reza Pahlavi had reigned since 1941; he died in exile in Cairo in 1980 and is buried there.

history.q: Which cleric returned from exile in February 1979 and became the Islamic Republic's first Supreme Leader?
history.fact: Ayatollah Khomeini had spent about 14 years in exile in Turkey, Iraq and France before returning to Tehran.

history.q: Which dynasty, founded by Shah Ismail I in 1501, made Twelver Shi'ism Iran's state religion?
history.fact: Ismail was only about 14 when he was crowned in Tabriz, which became the first Safavid capital.

history.q: Which ancient religion, founded by the prophet Zarathustra, was the official faith of the Sasanian kings?
history.fact: Zoroastrian fire temples still stand in Yazd, where one sacred flame is said to have burned for some 1,500 years.

history.q: Which Safavid ruler made Isfahan his capital in 1598?
history.fact: Abbas transformed the city around the vast Naqsh-e Jahan Square, inspiring the saying 'Isfahan is half the world'.

history.q: Which empire, the last great pre-Islamic Persian dynasty, fell to Arab Muslim armies in the 7th century?
history.fact: Founded by Ardashir I in 224 CE, the Sasanian Empire rivalled Rome and Byzantium for four centuries.

history.q: At Carrhae in 53 BCE, which Iranian empire's horse archers crushed the Roman general Crassus?
history.fact: The 'Parthian shot', fired backwards while riding away, is thought to have given English the phrase 'parting shot'.

history.q: Which Roman emperor was captured by the Sasanian king Shapur I in 260 CE?
history.fact: Shapur celebrated his triumph in rock reliefs at Naqsh-e Rostam, near Persepolis, showing Roman emperors submitting to him.

history.q: Which Mongol leader founded the Ilkhanate in Iran and took the Nizari fortress of Alamut in 1256?
history.fact: A grandson of Genghis Khan, Hulagu went on to sack Baghdad in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate there.

history.q: Which Iranian ruler sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried off the Mughal Peacock Throne?
history.fact: The loot also included the Koh-i-Noor diamond, which later passed to Afghan and Sikh rulers and then to the British.

history.q: Which dynasty made Tehran Iran's capital in 1786?
history.fact: Agha Mohammad Khan, founder of the Qajar dynasty, chose what was then a modest town near his tribe's northern homelands.

history.q: Long before the Persians, Susa was the capital of which ancient civilisation in south-western Iran?
history.fact: Hammurabi's famous law code was found at Susa in 1901, carried there as war booty by an Elamite king.

history.q: Which Achaemenid king was defeated by Alexander the Great at Gaugamela in 331 BCE?
history.fact: Darius III fled the battlefield and was killed the following year by one of his own satraps, Bessus.

history.q: Ecbatana, capital of the ancient Medes, lies beneath which modern Iranian city?
history.fact: Herodotus described Ecbatana ringed by seven walls of different colours, the innermost two plated in silver and gold.

history.q: Which British officer copied the Behistun Inscription of Darius I in the 1830s and 1840s, helping to crack cuneiform?
history.fact: The inscription, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, is carved about 100 m up a cliff; Rawlinson climbed with ropes and ladders to copy it.

history.q: Which Persian vizier of the Seljuk sultans founded the Nizamiyya network of colleges in the 11th century?
history.fact: He also wrote the 'Siyasatnama', a classic book of advice on statecraft, before his assassination in 1092.

history.q: At which 1514 battle did Ottoman Sultan Selim I's artillery defeat Shah Ismail I?
history.fact: The defeat briefly cost the Safavids their capital, Tabriz, and helped shape the long Ottoman-Iranian frontier.

history.q: A nationwide boycott in 1891-92 forced Naser al-Din Shah to cancel a British concession over which commodity?
history.fact: After a leading cleric issued a fatwa against its use, even the shah's own household reportedly gave it up until the concession was cancelled.

history.q: Karim Khan Zand, who styled himself 'Vakil' (regent) rather than shah, ruled from which city?
history.fact: He endowed Shiraz with a citadel, bazaar and bathhouse that still stand at the city's heart.

history.q: Which Sasanian king, the last of his dynasty, was killed near Merv in 651 while fleeing the Arab conquest?
history.fact: His death ended four centuries of Sasanian rule; his son Peroz later sought help at the court of Tang China.

technology.q: The word 'algorithm' comes from the name of which Persian mathematician of Baghdad's House of Wisdom?
technology.fact: His book 'al-Jabr' also gave us 'algebra'; his name points to Khwarazm, a region of Central Asia south of the Aral Sea.

technology.q: Which Persian polymath wrote 'The Canon of Medicine' and lies buried in Hamadan?
technology.fact: Born near Bukhara around 980, Avicenna saw his Canon used as a medical textbook in Europe for centuries.

technology.q: How did ancient Persians bring water from mountain aquifers to desert towns?
technology.fact: Some qanats run for tens of kilometres; UNESCO listed eleven Persian qanats as a World Heritage Site in 2016.

technology.q: The desert city of Yazd is famous for tall towers that funnel breezes down to cool houses. What are they called?
technology.fact: Badgirs catch even faint winds and push out hot air, a form of natural air conditioning used for centuries.

technology.q: Which Achaemenid highway, with relay stations for royal couriers, ran about 2,700 km from Sardis to Susa?
technology.fact: Herodotus praised couriers whom neither snow nor rain could stop, words later carved on New York's main post office.

technology.q: Which Tehran-born mathematician became the first woman to win the Fields Medal, in 2014?
technology.fact: As a teenager Mirzakhani won gold at the International Mathematical Olympiad twice, with a perfect score in 1995.

technology.q: What was a 'yakhchal' in the Iranian desert?
technology.fact: Its thick conical walls of heat-resistant mud brick stored ice made on winter nights, keeping it frozen into summer.

technology.q: Which Iranian-born engineer became the first woman to pay her own way to the International Space Station, in 2006?
technology.fact: Born in Mashhad, Anousheh Ansari also co-sponsored the Ansari X Prize for private spaceflight.

technology.q: Which resource was first struck commercially in the Middle East at Masjed Soleyman, Iran, in 1908?
technology.fact: The find led to the creation of the Anglo-Persian Oil Company, which much later became BP.

technology.q: Which physician from Rey, near Tehran, wrote the first known clinical account distinguishing smallpox from measles?
technology.fact: Al-Razi ran hospitals in Rey and Baghdad and reportedly chose a hospital site by hanging meat around the city to see where it rotted slowest.

technology.q: Which poet-mathematician from Nishapur helped devise the highly accurate Jalali calendar in the 11th century?
technology.fact: Khayyam also solved cubic equations geometrically, though abroad he is best known for the quatrains of the 'Rubaiyat'.

technology.q: Nasir al-Din Tusi founded a famous observatory in 1259 in which north-western Iranian town?
technology.fact: Funded by Hulagu Khan, it had a great library, and its astronomers devised models later echoed in Copernicus's work.

technology.q: Lotfi Zadeh, who grew up in Tehran, is famous for founding which field?
technology.fact: Born in Baku in 1921, Zadeh studied at the University of Tehran before a long career at UC Berkeley.

technology.q: Iran's South Pars is part of the world's largest natural gas field, shared with which country?
technology.fact: Qatar calls its side the North Field; the whole reservoir lies beneath the waters of the Persian Gulf.

technology.q: Which car, based on the British Hillman Hunter, was Iran's best-known home-built car for decades?
technology.fact: Built by Iran Khodro from 1967 to 2005, the Paykan, meaning 'arrow', was a familiar sight in Tehran's taxi fleet.

technology.q: The ancient windmills of Nashtifan in north-eastern Iran have what unusual feature?
choices: They are built entirely of stone
They spin on a vertical axis
technology.fact: Built of clay, straw and wood, these windmills still grind grain using the region's fierce '120-day winds'.

technology.q: What was the name of the first satellite Iran launched on its own rocket, in 2009?
technology.fact: Omid, meaning 'hope', was carried into orbit by a Safir rocket in February 2009.

technology.q: In traditional Iranian towns, what is an 'ab anbar'?
technology.fact: Often domed and cooled by windcatchers, ab anbars stored water underground; one in Yazd has six windcatchers.

technology.q: Which Tehran-born physicist co-invented the helium-neon gas laser in 1960?
technology.fact: Ali Javan's laser, built at Bell Labs, was the first to produce a continuous beam, paving the way for devices like barcode scanners.

technology.q: Which Tabriz-born scientist explained the rainbow around 1300 by experimenting with a glass sphere filled with water?
technology.fact: Al-Farisi showed that light is refracted twice and reflected once inside each raindrop to form the primary bow.

technology.q: Which mathematician from Kashan calculated pi to 16 decimal places in 1424?
technology.fact: Al-Kashi worked at Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand; his record for pi stood for about 170 years.

technology.q: According to tradition, who built the Band-e Kaisar bridge-dam at Shushtar for Shapur I?
technology.fact: Part of Shushtar's UNESCO-listed hydraulic system, it carried traffic and raised river water for over 1,500 years.

technology.q: Which galaxy did Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi of Rey describe as a 'little cloud' in his Book of Fixed Stars of 964?
technology.fact: It is the earliest known written record of the Andromeda Galaxy; a lunar crater, Azophi, honours al-Sufi.

technology.q: Which Sasanian city in Khuzestan was famed for its academy and hospital, a great centre of medical learning?
technology.fact: Its scholars drew on Greek, Indian and Persian learning, and some of its physicians later served the Abbasid court in Baghdad.

technology.q: Which 10th-century mathematician from Buzhgan in Khorasan advanced spherical trigonometry and the tangent function?
technology.fact: Working in Baghdad, Abu al-Wafa also wrote practical arithmetic for scribes and a geometry handbook for craftsmen.

art.q: Which poet wrote the 'Shahnameh' (Book of Kings), Iran's national epic?
art.fact: Ferdowsi spent some 30 years on its roughly 50,000 couplets, using very few Arabic words to celebrate the Persian language.

art.q: Which 13th-century Persian poet's 'Masnavi' inspired the Mevlevi order of whirling dervishes?
art.fact: Rumi was born in 1207 in the eastern Persian world, probably at Balkh, and spent most of his life in Konya, in today's Turkey.

art.q: Which 14th-century poet's tomb in Shiraz draws visitors who open his Divan at random to tell their fortunes?
art.fact: This custom, 'fal-e Hafez', is especially popular on Yalda Night, the longest night of the year.

art.q: Which Iranian director's 'A Separation' won the Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film in 2012?
art.fact: Farhadi won the same Academy Award again in 2017 for 'The Salesman'.

art.q: Naqsh-e Jahan Square, ringed by the Shah Mosque and Ali Qapu Palace, is in which city?
art.fact: Laid out by Shah Abbas I around 1600, it is one of the largest city squares in the world and once served as a polo field.

art.q: Which Achaemenid ceremonial capital features the Gate of All Nations and the Apadana's carved staircases?
art.fact: The Apadana reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts, from Ethiopians to Indians.

art.q: Isfahan's Si-o-se-pol bridge is named after its number of arches. How many are there?
art.fact: Built around 1602 for Shah Abbas I, it spans the Zayanderud river and doubles as a promenade and meeting place.

art.q: Edward FitzGerald's 1859 English version made which Persian poet's 'Rubaiyat' world famous?
art.fact: Lines such as 'A Jug of Wine, a Loaf of Bread—and Thou' became some of the most quoted verses in English.

art.q: A classic Persian 'chahar bagh' garden is divided by water channels into how many parts?
art.fact: Chahar bagh means 'four gardens'; UNESCO listed nine Persian gardens, including Fin Garden in Kashan, in 2011.

art.q: Which Iranian director won the Palme d'Or at Cannes in 1997 for 'Taste of Cherry'?
art.fact: He shared the prize with Japan's Shohei Imamura; Kiarostami was also a poet and photographer.

art.q: Which painter at Shah Abbas's court in Isfahan was famed for elegant single-figure miniatures of courtiers and youths?
art.fact: Reza Abbasi's lively drawings and portraits broke away from book illustration and were collected as individual album pages.

art.q: Which Shiraz mosque, nicknamed the 'Pink Mosque', is famed for morning light streaming through stained glass?
art.fact: Built in the 1880s under the Qajars, it fills with coloured light on winter mornings, when the sun is low.

art.q: Which Persian instrument is a trapezoid zither whose strings are struck with light wooden hammers?
art.fact: A typical santur has 72 strings, arranged in groups of four across movable bridges.

art.q: Which master singer, who died in 2020, was the most celebrated voice of Persian classical music?
art.fact: Shajarian's recording of the prayer 'Rabbana' was broadcast at sunset during Ramadan for decades.

art.q: Which 13th-century poet of Shiraz wrote the 'Gulistan' (Rose Garden) and the 'Bustan' (Orchard)?
art.fact: His poem 'Bani Adam', which says all people are limbs of one body, is quoted around the world.

art.q: Which poet of Nishapur wrote 'The Conference of the Birds', about birds seeking their king, the Simurgh?
art.fact: Thirty birds finish the journey and find the Simurgh is themselves: 'si murgh' means 'thirty birds' in Persian.

art.q: Which director made 'Children of Heaven', the first Iranian film nominated for an Oscar?
art.fact: The 1997 film follows a brother and sister who secretly share one pair of shoes after he loses hers.

art.q: Which 16th-century Safavid carpet, now in London's V&A museum, is named after the shrine city it was made for?
art.fact: Dated 1539-40, it has around 26 million knots; its twin is in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art.

art.q: The mausoleum of the Ilkhan Oljeitu, crowned by one of the world's largest brick domes, stands at which site?
art.fact: Completed around 1313, its double-shelled dome rises about 50 m and influenced later domes, including the Taj Mahal's.

art.q: Which 11th-century tomb tower near the Caspian is celebrated as the tallest tower ever built purely of brick?
art.fact: Built in 1006-07 for the Ziyarid ruler Qabus, its star-shaped brick shaft is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

art.q: Which great stepped temple, built by the Elamites around 1250 BCE, is Iran's best-preserved ziggurat?
art.fact: Built by King Untash-Napirisha, it was among Iran's first three UNESCO World Heritage Sites, listed in 1979.

art.q: Which Qajar-era court painter, famed for realist works such as his painting of the Mirror Hall, founded an influential art school in Tehran?
art.fact: Kamal-ol-Molk studied Europe's old masters and brought academic realism to Iranian painting.

art.q: The Persian word 'kashi', for glazed tile, comes from which city famed for medieval lustreware?
art.fact: Kashan's potters made shimmering lustre tiles and bowls in the 12th-14th centuries, prized across the Islamic world.

art.q: The traditional repertoire of melodies at the heart of Persian classical music, inscribed by UNESCO in 2009, is called what?
art.fact: Musicians memorise the radif's hundreds of short melodies, called gushehs, grouped into modal systems known as dastgahs.

art.q: Which 14th-century calligrapher is traditionally credited with creating the flowing Nastaliq script?
art.fact: Nastaliq, often called the 'bride of calligraphy', became the favourite script for Persian poetry; Mir Emad later perfected it.

politics.q: Which city is Iran's capital?
politics.fact: Tehran sits at the foot of the Alborz mountains; Mount Damavand, Iran's highest peak, can be seen from the city on clear days.

politics.q: Under the constitution of the Islamic Republic, what is the title of the country's highest authority?
politics.fact: The post was created by the 1979 constitution; Iran also has an elected president who heads the government.

politics.q: What is Iran's parliament commonly called?
politics.fact: Its full name is the Islamic Consultative Assembly, and its members are elected for four-year terms.

politics.q: In which year did a national referendum establish the Islamic Republic of Iran?
politics.fact: The Islamic Republic was proclaimed on 1 April 1979, a date marked each year as Islamic Republic Day.

politics.q: Which army officer founded the Pahlavi dynasty in 1925?
politics.fact: Reza Shah's government built the Trans-Iranian Railway, linking the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf, completed in 1938.

politics.q: Iran was one of the five founding members of which organisation, created in Baghdad in 1960?
politics.fact: OPEC's other founders were Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela.

politics.q: Which 1943 wartime conference first brought Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin together, in Iran's capital?
politics.fact: The 'Big Three' met at the Soviet embassy in Tehran and agreed on the Allied invasion of France planned for 1944.

politics.q: Who succeeded Ayatollah Khomeini as Supreme Leader in 1989?
politics.fact: Before that, Ali Khamenei had served two terms as Iran's president, from 1981 to 1989.

politics.q: How long is a single term for Iran's president?
politics.fact: Under the constitution, a president may serve no more than two consecutive terms.

politics.q: Which prime minister nationalised Iran's oil industry in 1951?
politics.fact: Mosaddegh was Time magazine's Man of the Year for 1951; he was overthrown in a 1953 coup backed by the US and Britain.

politics.q: Iran's first parliament opened in 1906 as a result of which movement?
politics.fact: Merchants, clerics and intellectuals took part, thousands of them by taking sanctuary (bast) in the grounds of the British legation in Tehran.

politics.q: Which 12-member body vets election candidates and reviews laws passed by Iran's parliament?
politics.fact: Six members are Islamic jurists chosen by the Supreme Leader; six are lawyers nominated by the judiciary and approved by parliament.

politics.q: Which elected body of clerics has the constitutional power to appoint the Supreme Leader?
politics.fact: Its members are chosen by popular vote for eight-year terms.

politics.q: Which president, elected in 1997, proposed the 'Dialogue Among Civilizations' that the UN adopted as its theme for 2001?
politics.fact: Khatami served two terms, from 1997 to 2005; earlier he had headed Iran's National Library.

politics.q: In which year did Iran become a founding member of the United Nations?
politics.fact: Iran was among the 51 original member states of the UN, which was founded in 1945.

politics.q: In which year did Reza Shah abdicate after British and Soviet forces entered Iran?
politics.fact: His son Mohammad Reza succeeded him at 21; Reza Shah died in exile in Johannesburg in 1944.

politics.q: What name was given to the Shah's 1963 reform programme, which included land reform and votes for women?
politics.fact: Approved in a referendum in January 1963, it redistributed land from large estates and extended the vote to women.

politics.q: How many provinces is Iran divided into?
politics.fact: The newest, Alborz, was carved out of Tehran Province in 2010, with Karaj as its capital.

politics.q: Who was elected the Islamic Republic's first president, in January 1980?
politics.fact: Banisadr was removed from office by parliament in June 1981 and spent the rest of his life in France.

politics.q: Who served as Iran's president from 1989 to 1997, focusing on reconstruction after the Iran-Iraq War?
politics.fact: Before becoming president, Rafsanjani was speaker of parliament for nine years, from 1980 to 1989.

politics.q: Which 1907 agreement divided Iran into Russian and British spheres of influence?
politics.fact: Russia took the north, Britain the south-east, and a neutral zone lay between, all without consulting Iran's government.

politics.q: Under which 1828 treaty did Qajar Iran cede Erivan and Nakhchivan to Russia?
politics.fact: The treaty fixed much of the new border along the Aras River and granted Russian subjects special legal privileges in Iran.

politics.q: How many times is the phrase 'Allahu Akbar' written in stylised script along the edges of Iran's flag?
politics.fact: The 22 repetitions recall 22 Bahman in the Iranian calendar, the date in 1979 marked as the revolution's victory.

politics.q: Which post was abolished by the 1989 revision of Iran's constitution?
politics.fact: Its executive powers were merged into the presidency, which has led the government ever since.

politics.q: Which Qajar shah signed Iran's first constitution in December 1906, days before his death?
politics.fact: His successor, Mohammad Ali Shah, had the parliament shelled in 1908 and was deposed by constitutionalists the following year.

current-affairs.q: In May 2024, Iranian President Ebrahim Raisi died in what kind of accident?
current-affairs.fact: The crash in fog-covered mountains of East Azerbaijan province also killed Foreign Minister Hossein Amir-Abdollahian.

current-affairs.q: Who won Iran's presidential election in July 2024?
current-affairs.fact: A heart surgeon from Mahabad who had served as health minister, Pezeshkian took office at the end of July 2024.

current-affairs.q: At the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, Iran won 2-0 against which team?
current-affairs.fact: Both goals, by Rouzbeh Cheshmi and Ramin Rezaeian, came deep in stoppage time.

current-affairs.q: In March 2025, Iran qualified for which FIFA World Cup?
current-affairs.fact: It was the seventh time Iran had qualified for a World Cup, and the fourth in a row since 2014.

current-affairs.q: Javad Foroughi, a 41-year-old nurse, won Olympic gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 in which event?
current-affairs.fact: It was Iran's first ever Olympic medal in shooting, and he set an Olympic record in the final.

current-affairs.q: Which sport, a national passion, gave Iran two of its three gold medals at the Paris 2024 Olympics?
current-affairs.fact: Saeid Esmaeili and Mohammad Hadi Saravi won Greco-Roman titles, while Arian Salimi took gold in taekwondo.

current-affairs.q: Who was elected president of Iran in June 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Raisi, previously head of the judiciary, succeeded Hassan Rouhani, who had served two terms.

current-affairs.q: In 2022, UNESCO inscribed which winter-solstice celebration of Iran and Afghanistan on its intangible heritage list?
current-affairs.fact: On Yalda, the longest night of the year, families stay up late eating pomegranates and watermelon and reading Hafez.

current-affairs.q: Which 1,394-km line, linking the Caspian Sea to the Persian Gulf, became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Built from 1927 to 1938, it crosses mountains and plains through 224 tunnels, some of them spirals.

current-affairs.q: Mehdi Taremi's bicycle kick for Porto against Chelsea in April 2021 was a finalist for which FIFA prize?
current-affairs.fact: The award, for the year's most beautiful goal, went to Tottenham's Erik Lamela for his rabona.

current-affairs.q: Which Asghar Farhadi film shared the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Set in Shiraz, it follows a prisoner on leave who tries to return a lost bag of gold coins.

current-affairs.q: In 2023 UNESCO listed 54 historic roadside inns from across Iran as a single World Heritage Site. What are they called?
current-affairs.fact: Built along trade and pilgrimage routes, these fortified inns sheltered travellers and their animals about a day's journey apart.

current-affairs.q: Which ancient broadleaf forests along the Caspian Sea became a UNESCO natural World Heritage Site in 2019?
current-affairs.fact: These forests date back 25 to 50 million years, to a time when such woodland covered much of the northern temperate zone.

current-affairs.q: In 2020, Iran, Azerbaijan, Turkey and Uzbekistan jointly won UNESCO intangible heritage status for which art?
current-affairs.fact: Persian miniatures illustrate poems and histories in jewel-like colours, painted with the finest of brushes.

current-affairs.q: On 1 January 2024, Iran officially joined which group of emerging economies, alongside Egypt, Ethiopia and the UAE?
current-affairs.fact: The name comes from its five members before 2024: Brazil, Russia, India and China, which founded it, and South Africa, which joined in 2010.

current-affairs.q: In December 2021, which Iranian-born chess prodigy became the youngest player ever to reach a 2800 rating?
current-affairs.fact: Born in Babol in 2003, Firouzja passed the mark aged 18, beating Magnus Carlsen's record; he has represented France since 2021.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Sajjad Ganjzadeh won Iran a gold medal in which sport, then making its Olympic debut?
current-affairs.fact: He won the men's over-75 kg kumite title; Iran's three golds in Tokyo came in shooting, wrestling and karate.

current-affairs.q: In July 2023, Iran became a full member of which Eurasian bloc at a summit hosted online by India?
current-affairs.fact: Founded in 2001, the SCO's members include China, Russia, India, Pakistan and several Central Asian states.

current-affairs.q: Who served as Iran's acting president after Ebrahim Raisi's death in May 2024?
current-affairs.fact: As first vice-president, Mokhber held the post under the constitution until a new president was elected within 50 days.

current-affairs.q: In July 2024, Masoud Pezeshkian won a presidential run-off against which candidate?
current-affairs.fact: Pezeshkian won about 54% of the vote in the second round, held on 5 July 2024.

current-affairs.q: Who became Iran's foreign minister in August 2024?
current-affairs.fact: A career diplomat, Araghchi had earlier served as deputy foreign minister and as ambassador to Japan.

current-affairs.q: Which mountainous Kurdish landscape of stepped villages was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021?
current-affairs.fact: Its villages climb such steep slopes that the roof of one house often serves as the yard of the house above.

current-affairs.q: In July 2025, UNESCO added the prehistoric caves and rock shelters of which valley to the World Heritage List?
current-affairs.fact: Its caves, such as Yafteh, preserve traces of Palaeolithic hunter-gatherers going back tens of thousands of years.

current-affairs.q: At the AFC Asian Cup in February 2024, Iran knocked out which tournament favourite in the quarter-finals?
current-affairs.fact: Iran came from behind to win 2-1 with a stoppage-time penalty, before losing a five-goal semi-final to hosts Qatar.

current-affairs.q: At the Tokyo Olympics in 2021, Mohammad Reza Geraei won gold in which style of wrestling?
current-affairs.fact: Greco-Roman wrestlers may not attack below the waist; Pahlavani, the fourth option, is Iran's ancient heroic style.

society.q: Iranians usually quote prices in tomans rather than rials. One toman equals how many rials?
society.fact: Shops, taxis and property adverts almost all use tomans, so a visitor reading a price tag has to multiply by ten to get the official rial figure.

society.q: In November 2019, a sudden overnight rise in the price of which product triggered nationwide protests in Iran?
society.fact: The rationed petrol price rose by 50% and the unrationed price tripled, announced with no warning at midnight on 15 November 2019.

society.q: Iran's economy has been squeezed by sanctions reimposed after the United States withdrew in 2018 from which agreement?
society.fact: The rial lost most of its value against the dollar in the years after the 2018 withdrawal, feeding persistent double-digit inflation.

society.q: In the 2020s, which country has been by far the largest buyer of Iranian oil?
society.fact: Independent 'teapot' refineries in China's Shandong province take most of the crude, often routed through intermediaries despite US sanctions.

society.q: In 2024 and 2025, Iranian authorities repeatedly closed government offices and schools for days to save what?
society.fact: Rolling blackouts hit homes and factories in summer and winter alike, as ageing power plants and gas shortages failed to keep pace with demand.

society.q: By 2023, Iran's population was closest to which figure?
society.fact: Iran's population has more than doubled since the 1979 revolution, although growth has slowed sharply as the birth rate has fallen.

society.q: In 2023, Iran's official annual inflation rate was closest to which figure?
society.fact: Food prices rose even faster than the headline rate, and Iran has had one of the highest inflation rates in the world since 2018.

society.q: Iran holds the world's second-largest reserves of which fuel, yet suffered winter shortages of it in 2024?
society.fact: Only Russia has larger gas reserves, but under-investment and heavy domestic use left Iran burning fuel oil in power plants to cope.

society.q: Which large salt lake in north-western Iran has shrunk dramatically since the 1990s, prompting a national restoration effort?
society.fact: Once one of the largest salt lakes on Earth, Urmia lost about 90% of its area by 2015, with salt storms affecting nearby farms and towns.

society.q: In May 2020, Iran's parliament approved a plan to rename the currency the toman and remove how many zeros from the rial?
society.fact: The redenomination was planned to take several years to phase in; a renewed version was approved again in 2025.

society.q: In December 2024, Iran lifted its block on which messaging app, which had been restricted since 2022?
society.fact: The Supreme Council of Cyberspace unblocked WhatsApp and Google Play; Telegram, blocked since 2018, remained restricted.

society.q: On taking office in 2021, President Ebrahim Raisi pledged to build how many new homes a year to tackle Iran's housing crisis?
society.fact: The 'National Housing Movement' targeted four million homes in four years; construction lagged far behind the goal as building costs soared.

society.q: In 2022, Iran approved resuming imports of which consumer product, banned since 2018 to save foreign currency?
society.fact: The ban left domestic makers Iran Khodro and Saipa with little competition; the first imported cars arrived in 2023.

society.q: In May 2025, which group of workers held a nationwide strike across Iran over fuel costs, insurance and low rates?
society.fact: The strike spread to dozens of cities within days, disrupting deliveries, and followed earlier proposals to raise diesel prices.

society.q: Iran's official overall unemployment rate in 2023 was closest to which figure?
society.fact: The headline figure masks far higher joblessness among graduates and young people, and a labour force participation rate of only about 40%.

society.q: By 2020, Iran's fertility rate had fallen to roughly how many children per woman?
society.fact: The rate was above six in the early 1980s; its rapid fall prompted the government to drop family-planning programmes and push pro-natal policies.

society.q: What do Iranians call the monthly cash payment the state has made to most citizens since subsidies were cut in 2010?
society.fact: Inflation eroded the original 455,000-rial payment; new, larger payments were added in 2022 after food import subsidies were removed.

society.q: In which Iranian city are schools and offices regularly closed for days each winter because of severe air pollution?
society.fact: Tehran's mountain-ringed basin traps smog from old vehicles and, in gas-short winters, from power plants burning fuel oil.

society.q: In 2022, Iran scrapped a preferential exchange rate of about how many rials to the US dollar used for importing essential goods?
society.fact: The rate had been introduced in 2018; its removal in May 2022 caused the price of flour-based foods and cooking oil to jump sharply.

society.q: Since the 2019 reform, Iranian private motorists have received a monthly quota of how many litres of petrol at the cheapest subsidised price?
society.fact: Drivers use a 'fuel card' at the pump; the quota price of 15,000 rials a litre stayed among the lowest in the world for years.

society.q: In March 2022, Iran's Supreme Labour Council raised the monthly minimum wage by roughly what percentage?
society.fact: The 57% rise was the largest in decades, but employers' groups objected and inflation soon ate into the gain.

society.q: What was the name of the law passed by Iran's parliament in 2021 to raise the birth rate?
choices: Youthful Population and Protection of the Family
society.fact: The law offered loans and housing perks to parents and restricted the free distribution of contraceptives in the public health system.

society.q: In the early 2020s, women's labour force participation in Iran was closest to which figure?
society.fact: The rate is among the lowest in the world even though women make up more than half of Iran's university students.

society.q: In 2024, Iran raised its value-added tax rate from 9% to what?
society.fact: The one-point rise took effect with the Iranian year starting in March 2024, as the state sought revenue to offset lower oil income.

society.q: In November 2021, farmers in Isfahan held large protests in the dried-up bed of which river?
society.fact: Water from the river had been diverted to industry and other provinces; its famous Isfahan bridges now often stand over dry ground.

general.q: What is the Persian New Year, celebrated at the spring equinox, called?
general.fact: Nowruz means 'new day'; it has been celebrated for over 3,000 years and is marked by some 300 million people from the Balkans to Central Asia.

general.q: What is Iran's official language?
general.fact: Persian is written in an Arabic-based script, but it is an Indo-European language, distantly related to English.

general.q: What is Iran's official currency?
general.fact: In everyday speech Iranians often count prices in 'tomans', each worth ten rials.

general.q: Which snow-capped volcano in the Alborz range is Iran's highest mountain?
general.fact: Rising about 5,610 m, Damavand is the highest volcano in Asia and features in Persian legend and the Shahnameh.

general.q: Iran produces the large majority of the world's supply of which precious spice?
general.fact: Each crocus flower yields just three red stigmas, picked by hand; Khorasan in north-east Iran is the heart of the harvest.

general.q: Which body of water, the largest lake on Earth, lies along Iran's northern coast?
general.fact: The Caspian is famous for sturgeon and caviar, and Iran's green shores in Gilan and Mazandaran grow rice and tea.

general.q: Which long-haired cat breed takes its name from Iran's old name in the West?
general.fact: Long-haired cats were brought from Persia to Europe in the 17th century, and the breed became a Victorian favourite.

general.q: What is the prized crispy golden layer of rice from the bottom of the pot called in Persian cooking?
general.fact: Tahdig means 'bottom of the pot'; families often compete politely for the last crunchy piece.

general.q: Which horseback ball game is believed to have originated in ancient Persia?
general.fact: Isfahan's Naqsh-e Jahan Square still has its old stone goalposts, and Persian polo, chogan, is on UNESCO's heritage list.

general.q: The chess word 'check' comes from which Persian word, meaning 'king'?
general.fact: Chess reached Persia from India as 'chatrang'; Persians passed it on to the Arab world, and from there it spread to Europe.

general.q: Which English word comes from an Old Iranian term for a walled enclosure or park?
general.fact: Greek writers borrowed 'paradeisos' for the walled parks of Persian kings, and the word came to mean heaven.

general.q: Which city is home to the vast shrine of Imam Reza, Iran's most visited pilgrimage site?
general.fact: Imam Reza is the only one of Shi'a Islam's Twelve Imams buried in Iran, and millions of pilgrims visit each year.

general.q: Which Iranian desert has recorded some of the hottest land-surface temperatures ever measured by satellite?
general.fact: Satellites measured about 70.7°C on its dark gravel plains in 2005; the Lut became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

general.q: What makes up the 'haft-sin' table laid out for Nowruz?
general.fact: Typical items include sabzeh (sprouts), sib (apple), sir (garlic), serkeh (vinegar) and sekkeh (coins).

general.q: Which Persian stew combines chicken or duck with ground walnuts and pomegranate molasses?
general.fact: Fesenjan's sweet-and-sour sauce is slow-cooked until dark and glossy; it is a festive favourite, especially on Yalda Night.

general.q: Which Tehran landmark, built in 1971 and first named the Shahyad Tower, marks the western entrance to the city?
general.fact: Designed by architect Hossein Amanat, it blends Sasanian and Islamic forms; its name means 'Freedom Tower'.

general.q: What is the popular nickname of Iran's national football team?
general.fact: 'Melli' simply means 'national'; Iran made its World Cup debut in Argentina in 1978.

general.q: Which salt lake in north-western Iran is famous for its flamingos and pink-tinted waters?
general.fact: Lake Urmia has shrunk dramatically since the 1990s, but salt-loving algae still tint parts of it red and pink.

general.q: Which freestyle wrestler, Olympic champion in 1956, is revered in Iran as 'Jahan Pahlavan' (World Champion)?
general.fact: Takhti was loved as much for his chivalry as his medals: gold in Melbourne in 1956 and silver in 1952 and 1960.

general.q: The modern Persian alphabet adds four letters to the Arabic script. How many letters does it have?
general.fact: The extra letters, for the sounds p, ch, zh and g, are made by adding dots or strokes to Arabic letters.

general.q: Which village near Tabriz has homes carved into cone-shaped volcanic rocks, much like Cappadocia?
general.fact: Kandovan's rock cones formed from the ash of nearby Mount Sahand, and families still live inside them.

general.q: Which Bronze Age 'Burnt City' in Sistan revealed what may be the world's oldest artificial eyeball?
general.fact: Found in a woman's grave, the eye was made of a light paste, possibly bitumen, and dates to around 2900-2800 BCE.

general.q: Which small Persian Gulf island near Bandar Abbas is famed for multicoloured mineral soils, including a red earth used as a spice?
general.fact: Locals use the red ochre soil, called gelak, in sauces and pickles, and the island's beaches glitter with mineral sand.

general.q: Which Caspian city was named a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy in 2015?
general.fact: Rasht is the capital of Gilan, famous for dishes full of herbs, garlic, sour plums and Caspian fish.

general.q: What is the traditional Iranian gymnasium, where athletes train with wooden clubs to drumbeats and poetry, called?
general.fact: Zurkhaneh means 'house of strength'; its rituals, known as Pahlavani, were inscribed by UNESCO in 2010.
